questions.stem: Three otherwise eligible adults apply for an initial Massachusetts pharmacy technician license. All meet the age, education, and moral-character requirements and have no disqualifying drug-related felony. Which applicants meet one of the educational or credential pathways in 247 CMR 8.02(3)(e)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Applicant A holds current certification from a Board-approved national pharmacy technician certifying body.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.02(3)(e)1 recognizes certification by a Board-approved certifying body as one pathway.

choices.text: Applicant B worked 410 hours as a technician trainee and passed a Board-approved technician assessment, but completed no approved training program.
choices.why: Incorrect. The hours-based path needs at least 500 documented trainee hours plus an approved exam; 410 without an approved training program is insufficient.

choices.text: Applicant C holds an active license from another state whose technician standards are substantially equivalent to Massachusetts and is in good standing.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.02(3)(e)2 permits the substantially equivalent, good-standing out-of-state licensure pathway.

choices.text: Applicant D passed a Board-approved assessment after 540 hours as a trainee, attested to under penalties of perjury and witnessed by the employer.
choices.why: Correct. The 500-hour trainee path combined with Board-approved examination and proper attestation meets 8.02(3)(e)3.b.

choices.text: Applicant E worked 150 hours at a pharmacy but holds no accepted certification or out-of-state license and did not pass a Board-approved examination.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ordinary unexamined job experience alone does not satisfy one of the listed 8.02(3)(e) alternatives.

questions.material_novelty: Compares distinct initial-license qualifying pathways rather than drug-felony eligibility, trainee employment maximum, or loss of existing certification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If B completes at least 500 acceptable trainee hours with the required employer-attested documentation, that applicant could satisfy the examination pathway.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy technician has not held an active state technician license for three full years. The technician submits the state renewal form and all ordinary back fees and assumes the Board must reinstate the license immediately without any additional conditions. What is the legally accurate next step?

choices.text: The pharmacist Manager of Record may independently waive all Board reinstatement conditions.
choices.why: Incorrect. An employer's approval is not the Board's determination of requirements following a long lapse.

choices.text: The Board may impose additional conditions before renewing a technician license that has lapsed for more than two years.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.07(4) gives the Board authority to require other conditions beyond an ordinary fee/application.

choices.text: The technician may resume certified duties upon payment alone even before the state license is renewed.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.07(2) treats practice after expiration as unlicensed.

choices.text: The license is permanently barred from any future renewal after exactly two calendar years.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule allows renewal subject to possible additional Board conditions; it does not impose automatic permanent disqualification.

choices.text: Active national certification automatically revives the expired Massachusetts technician license.
choices.why: Incorrect. National certification is separate from state licensure and does not negate 247 CMR 8.07(4).

questions.material_novelty: Tests additional Board conditions after a >2-year licensing lapse, not the birthday-based two-year expiration or certification status itself.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the state technician license only recently lapsed, subsection 8.07(4)'s special more-than-two-year condition is not triggered, though normal renewal requirements still apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern admits to knowingly falsifying required internship records. The Board finds the conduct violated applicable pharmacy law. The intern argues that the Board's only available remedy is to reject those particular hours, not affect pharmacist examination eligibility. Which statement is supported by 247 CMR 8.01(17)?

choices.text: The Board may disregard only the falsified hours because licensing misconduct never affects eligibility to sit for the pharmacist examination.
choices.why: Incorrect. The subsection expressly provides for a prohibition against taking the exam after regulatory misconduct.

choices.text: Every intern found responsible for any minor regulation violation must be permanently barred from the MPJE and NAPLEX.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision says the intern may be prohibited from taking the examination; permanent automatic bars are not prescribed in every case.

choices.text: Only the pharmacy employer, not the Board, may impose consequences for the internship fraud.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board retains licensing and examination eligibility authority over pharmacy interns.

choices.text: The intern may be prohibited from taking the licensing examination in addition to other sanctions the Board may impose.
choices.why: Correct. That is the specific possible consequence enumerated in 247 CMR 8.01(17).

choices.text: Exam eligibility is automatically restored if the intern promises to repay the pharmacy for the false hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. Private repayment does not supersede a Board sanction or its determination of eligibility.

questions.material_novelty: Tests a specifically authorized examination-eligibility sanction against pharmacy interns, distinct from pharmacist summary suspension or school withdrawal reporting.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no violation is found, subsection 8.01(17)'s misconduct-based examination prohibition is not established.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy operates its own on-the-job pharmacy technician and technician-trainee training program. The Board asks about the program after a technician reports that training was entirely informal and no guidelines exist. Which statements accurately describe 247 CMR 8.06(2)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Any pharmacy may train staff entirely by verbal tradition; no written guidelines are necessary when the trainer is a pharmacist.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 8.06(2) requires training programs to comply with the pharmacy's written guidelines.

choices.text: A pharmacist may train a technician or trainee in a proper on-the-job program under 247 CMR 8.00.
choices.why: Correct. This method of training is expressly contemplated by 247 CMR 8.06(2).

choices.text: The training program automatically converts an unlicensed worker into a licensed pharmacy technician without a Board application.
choices.why: Incorrect. An internal training program does not replace the applicable state licensure requirement.

choices.text: Program guidelines must be written to conform to professional, ethical, and legal pharmacy practice standards.
choices.why: Correct. Section 8.06(2) requires written guidelines consistent with those standards.

choices.text: The pharmacy must provide copies of its training-program guidelines to the Board upon request.
choices.why: Correct. The closing sentence of 8.06(2) makes the guidelines available on Board request.

questions.material_novelty: Focuses on the required written ON-THE-JOB training guidelines and Board access, not a listing of currently employed personnel or delegation scope.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A pharmacy with a documented compliant training program and available written guidelines would meet this specific section's policy condition.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist must determine which of the following ADHD medicines is federally Schedule II. Assume ordinary FDA-approved prescription products and no special exemptions. Which medication requires Schedule II controls?

choices.text: Strattera (atomoxetine).
choices.why: Incorrect. FDA labeling confirms atomoxetine is not a federally controlled substance.

choices.text: Intuniv (guanfacine extended-release).
choices.why: Incorrect. Guanfacine is not listed as a federal Schedule II controlled stimulant.

choices.text: Focalin (dexmethylphenidate).
choices.why: Correct. FDA Focalin labeling identifies dexmethylphenidate as Schedule II, consistent with the federal methylphenidate-related stimulant control.

choices.text: Kapvay (clonidine extended-release).
choices.why: Incorrect. Clonidine is a non-federally scheduled prescription drug.

choices.text: Qelbree (viloxazine extended-release).
choices.why: Incorrect. Viloxazine is an FDA-approved nonstimulant ADHD medicine rather than a federal Schedule II substance.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1308.12(d)(4); FDA Focalin labeling §9.1; FDA Strattera labeling §9.1; 105 CMR 700.002
questions.material_novelty: Tests dexmethylphenidate versus five ADHD-brand alternatives without giving the intended schedule in the stem; no previous A–D question names Focalin, Strattera or Qelbree.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the prescribed medicine is atomoxetine rather than dexmethylphenidate, Schedule II controls do not apply solely based on the ADHD diagnosis.

questions.stem: A pharmacist has valid prescriptions for Nucynta (tapentadol) and Ultram (tramadol). Both are ordinary approved single-ingredient oral prescription products. Which federal scheduling statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Nucynta/tapentadol is Schedule II and cannot be refilled on the original Schedule II prescription.
choices.why: Correct. Tapentadol is listed in 21 CFR 1308.12(c)(29) as Schedule II; Schedule II prescription refills are prohibited under 21 CFR 1306.12(a).

choices.text: Ultram/tramadol is Schedule II because every synthetic opioid has the same federal schedule.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tramadol is specifically Schedule IV under 21 CFR 1308.14(b)(3).

choices.text: Ultram/tramadol is Schedule IV, ordinarily subject to the federal six-month and five-refill limits for Schedule III–IV prescriptions.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 1308.14(b)(3) and 1306.22(a) establish the stated rules.

choices.text: The pharmacist can give Nucynta five refills by applying the federal Schedule IV refill rule to both medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Schedule III/IV refill limits cannot be applied to a Schedule II prescription.

choices.text: Nucynta is not controlled if the prescription is intended for short-term pain relief rather than long-term therapy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The intended pain-treatment duration does not change tapentadol's federal Schedule II classification.

questions.material_novelty: Uses previously untaught tapentadol/Nucynta identity and contrasts federal opioid schedules and distinct refill consequences, not another hydrocodone or tramadol-only recognition question.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Changing the Nucynta ingredient to tramadol would replace Schedule II with IV and allow only the Schedule IV-limited refill regime.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy receives a valid prescription written only for the GENERIC name of a drug. The prescriber has specified no manufacturer, but marks 'no substitution.' The pharmacist is choosing between lawfully marketed manufacturers of that same generic prescription product, consistent with the prescriber's intended formulation. What does 247 CMR 9.05(2) allow?

choices.text: The pharmacist must dispense nothing until the prescriber writes a particular manufacturer's name.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsection 9.05(2) expressly permits choosing among marketed products when the generic name is prescribed without a specified manufacturer.

choices.text: The pharmacist may select any therapeutic-class alternative even with a different active ingredient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescriber's intent and professional judgment still limit selection; the generic-name provision does not authorize therapeutic substitution.

choices.text: The pharmacist may choose a lawfully marketed product consistent with the prescription even if it is not on the MA List of Interchangeable Drugs, despite the generic order's 'no substitution' marking.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.05(2) explicitly allows this selection where no manufacturer was specified, regardless of interchange-list listing or a no-substitution notation.

choices.text: Only the pharmacy's highest-priced branded product is permissible if 'no substitution' appears.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.05(2) does not confine a nonspecific generic drug order to the highest-priced brand.

choices.text: The prescription becomes automatically invalid because 'no substitution' can never appear on a generic-name order.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule anticipates such a marking and specifically addresses the pharmacist's authority despite it.

questions.material_novelty: Examines generic-name prescriptions with no named manufacturer and a no-substitution notation; prior interchange cases were BRAND-written orders or brand-for-brand labeling.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the prescription specifies a particular manufacturer as part of its intent, the unrestricted manufacturer-choice premise of 9.05(2) does not apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy offers personal pharmacist counseling but posts only a small sign inside its locked dispensary, invisible to patients. Which corrections accurately reflect 247 CMR 9.18(7)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Use a conspicuous sign at least 11 inches high and 14 inches wide.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.18(7) prescribes a minimum 11-by-14-inch sign.

choices.text: Print the counseling-rights wording in letters at least one-half inch high.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.18(7) sets the minimum height of the sign's lettering.

choices.text: Place a sign adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, so customers can see their counseling rights.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.18(7) requires conspicuous placement beside each dispensing area.

choices.text: The pharmacy may omit the counseling-rights sign whenever a technician verbally offers counseling to each patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. A verbal offer does not waive the separate posted-sign requirement.

choices.text: Any sign promoting generic cost savings is an adequate replacement for the specified counseling-rights wording.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.18(7) supplies particular patient-rights information; a cost-savings advertisement is not a substitute.

questions.material_novelty: Tests mandated counseling-rights sign dimensions, lettering and placement, not the private consultation area's accessibility or individual pharmacist name tags.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A properly sized, legible counseling-rights sign prominently adjacent to the dispensing area cures the specific physical posting deficiency.

questions.topic: DUR drug-food interaction and documented response
questions.stem: A pharmacist receives a new prescription for a medicine with a clinically significant FOOD interaction. The patient says they take the interacting food every day, and a DUR alert is triggered. The pharmacist has not assessed the risk or informed the prescriber. The patient declines routine counseling and asks for immediate pickup. Which action best satisfies 247 CMR 9.17?

choices.text: Dispense without review because a patient's refusal of counseling also waives the prospective drug utilization review.
choices.why: Incorrect. A counseling refusal does not cancel the independent pharmacist prospective DUR duty.

choices.text: Ask the pharmacy cashier to decide whether the food interaction is important, then release the medication.
choices.why: Incorrect. Professional assessment of a clinically significant drug-food interaction remains the pharmacist's responsibility.

choices.text: Allow the insurance company's paid claim to serve as the safety clearance for drug-food interactions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payment adjudication does not replace prospective clinical DUR.

choices.text: Evaluate the interaction before release, take appropriate patient/prescriber measures and document the DUR response.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 9.17(1)(e) and (2) explicitly address drug-food interactions, appropriate interventions and documentation.

choices.text: Wait to consider the food interaction until the patient's next annual medication review.
choices.why: Incorrect. The required DUR occurs before dispensing or delivery of the new order.

questions.material_novelty: Changes the dispositive hazard from known drug-drug/therapeutic duplication to food interaction and independently tests documentation despite counseling refusal.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no clinically significant interaction exists after a pharmacist DUR review, the need for intervention may differ; the DUR obligation remains.

questions.topic: Counseling access during all open hours
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy remains legally open for prescription services for the next hour. A patient collecting a new drug asks for pharmacist counseling on an important administration precaution. The pharmacy has a licensed pharmacist on the premises, but the cashier announces that counseling is available only at a weekly scheduled clinic and advises pickup now with counseling later. What does 247 CMR 9.18(8) require?

choices.text: An online pharmacy advertisement mentioning counseling is sufficient to replace actual availability while the pharmacy is open.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation specifies counseling availability throughout the pharmacy's business hours.

choices.text: The pharmacy must make pharmacist or pharmacy-intern counseling available while open and address the requested new-therapy counseling before release as applicable.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 9.18(3),(4),(8) require qualified counseling and availability at all times pharmacy services are open.

choices.text: Only patients receiving Schedule II medicines may request counseling during ordinary business hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. The counseling rights apply to prescriptions generally, not only Schedule II medications.

choices.text: A cashier may provide the complete pharmacologic counseling because the pharmacist is busy.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.18(3) prohibits technicians and other nonpharmacists from providing patient drug counseling.

choices.text: The patient must pay a separate counseling fee to obtain advice outside the weekly clinic schedule.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cited pharmacy rule does not condition required counseling availability on an appointment or such a fee.

questions.material_novelty: Tests continuous access to actual qualified counseling while the pharmacy remains open, distinct from posted-sign and physical private consultation area requirements.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy is closed and no prescription is being released, the open-hours requirement would not be triggered in the same way.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts physician is duly licensed and authorized for ordinary Schedule VI prescribing. The physician does not hold a DEA registration and is therefore automatically registered under Massachusetts law only for Schedule VI. Another clinic employee asks the pharmacist whether the same credentials authorize Schedule IV. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: For Schedule VI-only prescribing, the physician may use an applicable Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration number in the registration-number field instead of a nonexistent individual DEA number.
choices.why: Correct. The definition of Registration Number in 105 CMR 721.010 directs Schedule VI-only prescribers without a DEA number to use the Massachusetts MCSR number.

choices.text: A Schedule VI-only MCSR automatically authorizes the physician to prescribe Schedule IV medication without a DEA registration.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal Schedule IV prescribing requires appropriate DEA authority and state schedule authority.

choices.text: The duly licensed physician may issue an otherwise valid Schedule VI prescription under the state's automatic Schedule VI-only registration framework.
choices.why: Correct. 105 CMR 700.004(D)(1) provides automatic Schedule VI registration for a qualifying physician without DEA registration.

choices.text: The physician needs adequate state and federal authorization for Schedule IV, which is not established by the given Schedule VI-only credentials.
choices.why: Correct. 105 CMR 700.004(D) recognizes DEA schedule authority as a limit on automatic authorized schedules.

choices.text: A pharmacist may enter a colleague's unrelated DEA number on the Schedule VI prescription to make the original prescriber appear to have federal controlled-substance authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. Substituting someone else's registration identity would misrepresent the lawful issuing prescriber.

questions.citation: 105 CMR 700.004(D)(1); 105 CMR 721.010 definition of Registration Number; M.G.L. c.94C §18(a)
questions.material_novelty: Separates the authentic MCSR-as-registration-number path for Schedule VI-only Massachusetts physician from the separate DEA/MCSR requirements for Schedule II–V prescribing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the practitioner obtains proper DEA Schedule IV and matching state authorization, the restricted Schedule VI-only conclusion would no longer apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed INSTITUTIONAL STERILE COMPOUNDING pharmacy is reviewing which ordinary requirements under 247 CMR 9.04 apply to its setting. Other controlled-substance rules are evaluated separately. Which statements correctly distinguish the specific 9.04(15) exemption from duties that remain? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The 9.04(12) ordinary Schedule VI one-year validity/emergency-supply rule is among the enumerated exceptions for this license category.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection 9.04(15) explicitly exempts institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(12).

choices.text: The pharmacy remains covered by the general 9.04(1) duty to have a licensed pharmacist perform final dispensing process validation.
choices.why: Correct. The 9.04(15) list does not include subsection (1).

choices.text: The pharmacy remains subject to the computerized pharmacy-system requirement in 9.04(2) under this section.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection 9.04(2) is not among the enumerated 9.04(15) exemptions.

choices.text: The 9.04(14) customer-identifier pickup rule is one of the listed exceptions for an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. Subsection 9.04(15) expressly lists subsection (14).

choices.text: The institutional sterile compounding exemption eliminates every DEA and Massachusetts controlled-substance registration and storage obligation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The enumerated exceptions do not waive independent applicable federal or state controlled-substance obligations.

questions.material_novelty: Tests exactly which subsections of retail 9.04 are exempt for an institutional sterile compounding license, rather than ordinary retail refill expiry or pickup identification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the facility is a standard retail Drug Store Pharmacy rather than an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy, 9.04(15) cannot support the exemption.

questions.stem: A pharmacist processes a lawful refill of a Massachusetts Schedule VI maintenance medicine using an already authorized prescription. The refilled prescription is not federally controlled. Which records are required by the Massachusetts state refill rule, 247 CMR 9.04(6)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The date the refill medication is dispensed.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.04(6)(a) requires the dispensing date even for Schedule VI refills.

choices.text: The amount of medicine dispensed on the refill.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.04(6)(b) requires the quantity dispensed.

choices.text: The dispensing pharmacist's initials.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.04(6)(c) expressly requires the pharmacist's initials.

choices.text: A new written physician prescription for every refill despite remaining valid authorized refills.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule addresses documenting lawfully authorized refills, not mandating a replacement prescription each time.

choices.text: No refill record whatsoever, because Schedule VI is not controlled federally.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts Schedule VI remains subject to its state pharmacy record requirements.

questions.material_novelty: Applies the distinct Massachusetts Schedule VI refill record elements rather than federal 21 CFR 1306.22 Schedule III–V or Schedule VI validity duration.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the order is a newly issued initial prescription instead of a refill, the 9.04(6) refill documentation condition is not triggered in the same form.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy uses SINGLE-DRUG-SINGLE-DOSE solid oral packaging and wants to prepackage a known approved drug before receiving any patient-specific prescription. The pharmacy has appropriate packaging facilities and a pharmacist who will later conduct final validation. Which measures comply with 247 CMR 9.08(2)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Properly label each prepackaged single-drug dose before it is used for a patient.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(2)(b) requires properly labeled medications packaged before patient prescription receipt.

choices.text: Use barcode scanning or comparable identification technology at dispensing to verify the prepackaged medication.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(2)(b) requires scanning or a similar technology to verify the drug at dispensing.

choices.text: Treat the prepackaged unit as a valid prescription itself and release it to any patient without an authorized patient-specific order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Advance prepackaging does not create a patient-specific legal prescription or waive final validation.

choices.text: Prepackaging must be avoided entirely until after the individual prescription is received.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(2)(b) expressly permits prepackaging before a prescription if its safeguards are met.

choices.text: A supplier's purchase invoice alone satisfies the patient dispensing verification requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. An invoice does not meet the product identification technology requirement at dispensing.

questions.material_novelty: Tests **single-drug solid oral unit prepackaging before prescription receipt** and barcode identification at dispensing, versus prior multi-drug packaging or robotic verification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the prepackaged units are mislabeled or not identified by proper scanning at dispensing, the pre-prescription prepackaging process does not comply.

questions.topic: PRN drug in multi-drug compliance pouch
questions.stem: A pharmacy prepares weekly multi-drug-single-dose pouches for a patient. The pouch contains compatible scheduled daily Schedule IV and Schedule VI oral tablets. The prescriber now adds cyclobenzaprine 5 mg tablets to be taken ONLY AS NEEDED for muscle spasms. Assume all other compliance-packaging conditions are met. Which action is consistent with 247 CMR 9.08(3)?

choices.text: Include the as-needed tablets in each daily multi-drug dose because cyclobenzaprine is not federally scheduled.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(3)(c) excludes as-needed medicines regardless of their federal controlled schedule.

choices.text: Include a two-week supply of PRN tablets in the daily pouches if the patient signs an informed consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient approval does not waive the no-PRN-in-multi-drug-single-dose requirement.

choices.text: Move all current daily therapy to ordinary stock containers and discontinue any multi-drug compliance packaging.
choices.why: Incorrect. An as-needed prescription does not automatically prohibit packaging other compatible scheduled daily medicines.

choices.text: Keep the scheduled daily medicines in appropriate multi-drug-single-dose packages but dispense the PRN cyclobenzaprine separately.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(3)(c) bars PRN medicine in the multi-drug pack while otherwise eligible regular-dose products may remain.

choices.text: Use a 30-day beyond-use date for the PRN medicine and the packaging limitation no longer applies.
choices.why: Incorrect. Assigning a BUD does not turn an as-needed order into fixed daily dosing.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the PRN exclusion with an otherwise permitted daily Schedule IV/VI solid pack rather than the previously tested Schedule II/III exclusions or package BUD limits.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If cyclobenzaprine were prescribed as an appropriate fixed daily dose (rather than PRN) and all other requirements were met, this particular prohibition would not arise.

questions.topic: Removed medication from returned compliance packaging
questions.stem: A pharmacy accepts an eligible return of a multi-drug-single-dose pack it originally dispensed to Patient X. The patient's prescriber discontinued one medicine; the pharmacist correctly removes it and intends to repack and redispense the remaining medicines to Patient X. Which statements about the REMOVED medication and documentation are correct under 247 CMR 9.08(4)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The removed tablets cannot be returned to saleable pharmacy inventory.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(4)(b) expressly bars returning medication removed from the pack to inventory.

choices.text: The removed tablets may be dispensed to unrelated Patient Y after the pharmacist checks the strength.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(4)(b) prohibits dispensing removed medication to anyone other than the original patient who returned the pack.

choices.text: The pharmacy must document repackaging, removal and redispensing, including the identity of the pharmacist making the change.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(4)(c) requires an accountability record identifying the pharmacist.

choices.text: The changed package must be properly relabeled before being redispensed to Patient X.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(4)(a)3 requires labeling under 9.08(5) before redispensing.

choices.text: Returning a package to the original pharmacy transfers ownership of all removed doses to unrestricted distributable retail stock.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation permits limited same-patient repackaging, not generalized restocking.

questions.material_novelty: Tests disposition **of the removed tablets themselves** and pharmacist identification when adjusting returned packs, not whether the original pharmacy may repack for the same patient.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no dose is removed or redispensed and the pack never returned, the special return/repackaging accounting rule would not be triggered.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts applicant receives a NEW Drug Store Pharmacy license in 2026 and proposes a prescription area of 300 square feet. All other safety facilities, staffing and licensing conditions are satisfied. Is this prescription-area size compliant with 247 CMR 9.19(2)?

choices.text: Yes; 300 square feet is sufficient if a centrally monitored alarm is also installed.
choices.why: Incorrect. An alarm does not waive the specified minimum prescription-area floor space.

choices.text: Yes; the 325-square-foot rule applies only to pharmacies with sterile compounding authorizations.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly applies to Drug Store pharmacies licensed on or after July 1, 2020.

choices.text: No; a newly licensed Drug Store Pharmacy under that date rule must have a prescription area of at least 325 square feet.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(2) establishes a 325-square-foot minimum for Drug Store licenses obtained July 1, 2020 or later.

choices.text: No; all Massachusetts pharmacies, including nonresident facilities, must have at least 500 square feet.
choices.why: Incorrect. The given 9.19(2) threshold is 325 square feet; the rule has specific license/category exceptions.

choices.text: It is sufficient if the owner changes the construction drawing's label to 'consultation area'.
choices.why: Incorrect. Relabeling a physically undersized prescription area cannot satisfy the substantive space requirement.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the July 1, 2020 licensure-triggered physical 325-square-foot requirement, not sterile compounding licensure or facility credential display.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A genuine prescription area of at least 325 square feet would satisfy this particular size rule.

questions.stem: A resident Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy uses a new balance for customary simple nonsterile compounding. Management bought an expensive pharmacy-grade scale but never arranged testing or sealing by a weights-and-measures sealer and the scale is not labeled 'legal for trade.' Which conditions are specified by 247 CMR 9.19(1)(e)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The balance must accurately weigh quantities as small as ten milligrams.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(e) specifies a 10 mg minimum weighing capability.

choices.text: The balance must be tested and sealed by a state or local sealer of weights and measures at least once each calendar year.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(e) gives an explicit annual testing/sealing duty.

choices.text: Every newly acquired balance must bear a 'legal for trade' designation.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(e) requires that designation for all new balances.

choices.text: Only manufacturer calibration paperwork is needed; state or local testing is prohibited.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute specifically calls for state/local sealer testing and sealing, not an exclusive manufacturer certificate.

choices.text: An expensive digital display automatically exempts the balance from annual weights-and-measures testing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Purchase price and display technology are not listed exemptions under 9.19(1)(e).

questions.material_novelty: Tests resident retail balance capability and mandatory annual weights-and-measures sealing, rather than USP <795> batch-record equipment checks or veterinary reference lists.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the balance is newly compliant, 10 mg capable and annually tested/sealed by the appropriate authority, the specified issues are resolved.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts RESIDENT retail pharmacy wants to revise its controlled-drug stock security. The Manager of Record proposes storing Schedule II–V products only in a locked cabinet, while a second manager claims a separate Schedule II vault is always mandatory. Which statements correctly apply 247 CMR 9.21? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: All controlled substances, including Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drugs, must be stored in the secured prescription area in a safe and secure manner.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(1) covers all controlled substances, including those Massachusetts classifies as Schedule VI.

choices.text: Schedules II–V may be secured in a substantially constructed locked cabinet or similarly secured storage area, OR dispersed among Schedule VI stock so as to obstruct theft/diversion.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(2) expressly provides these storage alternatives.

choices.text: Federal Schedule II medicines must always be placed in a separate safe even when the pharmacy otherwise meets the cited secure dispersed-stock option.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(2) allows a secure dispersion alternative for Schedule II–V as written; other applicable rules still matter.

choices.text: The pharmacy must maintain a centrally monitored security system designed to detect security breaches and activate it when closed.
choices.why: Correct. This is expressly required by 247 CMR 9.21(3).

choices.text: Any shelf accessible from the supermarket's public aisle is permitted if a pharmacist works nearby.
choices.why: Incorrect. All controlled substances must remain in the secured prescription area, with effective diversion/theft protection.

questions.material_novelty: Distinguishes Massachusetts resident retail secure dispersion alternative from institutional hospital bulk vault rules and pharmacy-within-store barrier alarms.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the products are stored in public uncontrolled aisles, they do not satisfy the secured prescription-area requirement even if dispersed.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy employs several registered pharmacists, each with an individual NABP e-Profile number. The PHARMACY business itself has not established the national database identifier required by the Board. The owner argues that the staff members' personal identifiers satisfy every institutional requirement. What does 247 CMR 9.19(20) require?

choices.text: A pharmacy has no national-identifier obligation if every pharmacist holds a personal registration.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacy's facility-level identifier duty is separate from individual pharmacist personal requirements.

choices.text: The owner may instead post the manager's DEA number, which automatically serves as the facility's NABP e-Profile number.
choices.why: Incorrect. A DEA registration number is not the specified NABP or other Board-required national database identifier.

choices.text: The pharmacy must always obtain a separate identifier from every national pharmacy database, even when the Board names only one.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule describes an NABP e-Profile or another national database as required by the Board, not mandatory universal enrollment.

choices.text: A current Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy license alone automatically satisfies the express national database identifier duty.
choices.why: Incorrect. The state facility license does not replace the separate requirement under 9.19(20).

choices.text: The pharmacy itself must maintain an NABP e-Profile number or another Board-required national database identifier.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(20) specifies that facility-level duty distinct from 9.01(20) for individual pharmacists.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the separate facility national database ID, compared with a pharmacist's personal e-Profile and posted state pharmacy license already tested.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the facility obtains and maintains the Board-required national database identifier, individual pharmacist IDs remain separate but this facility deficiency is cured.
